Name: Oud
Description: A short-necked, fretless lute with a deep pear-shaped body. Central to classical and folk music across the Arab world, Turkey, Greece, and Central Asia.

Name: Sitar
Description: A long-necked plucked lute with movable frets and sympathetic strings, producing a rich, resonant tone. A defining instrument of North Indian (Hindustani) classical music.

Name: Kora
Description: A 21-string harp-lute made from a large gourd resonator covered in cowhide. Central to the MandÃ© griot tradition of West Africa.

Name: Guqin
Description: A seven-string fretless zither with a history spanning over 3,000 years. Revered in Chinese culture as an instrument of scholars and sages.

Name: Shamisen
Description: A three-stringed plucked lute with a square body covered in skin, played with a large plectrum. Used in Japanese kabuki, bunraku, and folk music.

Name: Koto
Description: A 13-string plucked zither placed horizontally, with movable bridges. A principal instrument of Japanese classical and contemporary music.

Name: Gayageum
Description: A 12-string plucked zither with silk or nylon strings. One of the most important instruments in Korean traditional music.

Name: Pipa
Description: A four-stringed pear-shaped lute played with fingernails. A major solo and ensemble instrument in Chinese classical music for over two thousand years.

Name: Charango
Description: A small ten-string lute traditionally made with an armadillo shell body. Iconic in Andean music across Bolivia, Peru, Ecuador, and northern Argentina.

Name: Bandurria
Description: A plucked string instrument with a flat back and 12 strings in 6 courses. Used in Spanish, Latin American, and Filipino rondalla ensembles.

Name: Cuatro
Description: A small four or five-stringed guitar-family instrument. Prominent in the folk and popular music of Venezuela, Puerto Rico, and other Caribbean nations.

Name: Tres
Description: A three-course plucked string instrument derived from the Spanish guitar. Fundamental to Cuban son and other Caribbean genres.

Name: Balalaika
Description: A triangular-bodied Russian stringed instrument with three strings. A symbol of Russian folk music, played solo and in orchestras.

Name: Domra
Description: A long-necked Russian lute with a round body and three or four strings. Used in Russian folk ensembles alongside the balalaika.

Name: Dombra
Description: A long-necked two-stringed lute and the national instrument of Kazakhstan. Used for solo kÃ¼y performances that narrate stories and depict nature.

Name: Komuz
Description: A three-stringed fretless lute and national instrument of Kyrgyzstan. Played with virtuosic plucking and strumming techniques.

Name: Tar
Description: A long-necked double-bellied lute carved from mulberry wood. A primary instrument of Azerbaijani mugham and Iranian classical music.

Name: Setar
Description: A delicate long-necked lute with four strings, played with the index finger. Used in Persian classical music for intimate solo performance.

Name: Tanbur
Description: A long-necked fretted lute found across Central Asia, Iran, and Turkey. Used in classical maqam and shashmaqam traditions.

Name: Saz (BaÄŸlama)
Description: A family of long-necked plucked lutes and the most widely played instrument in Turkish folk music. Features movable frets for microtonal intervals.

Name: Rubab
Description: A short-necked lute with a double-chambered body carved from mulberry wood. The national instrument of Afghanistan, considered an ancestor of the Indian sarod.

Name: Sarod
Description: A fretless plucked lute with a metal fingerboard, producing deep, sustained tones. A major solo instrument in Hindustani classical music.

Name: Veena (Saraswati)
Description: A large plucked lute with two gourd resonators. One of the oldest and most important instruments in South Indian (Carnatic) classical music.

Name: Ngoni
Description: A small plucked lute from West Africa with a wooden trough body and skin soundboard. Considered a precursor to the American banjo.

Name: Xalam
Description: A plucked lute from the Wolof and Fulani traditions of West Africa. A griot instrument used for praise singing and storytelling.

Name: Valiha
Description: A tubular bamboo zither of Austronesian origin and the national instrument of Madagascar. Strings are cut from the bamboo tube itself.

Name: Guzheng (Zheng)
Description: A large plucked zither with 21 or more strings and movable bridges. One of the most popular traditional Chinese instruments, with ancient origins.

Name: ÄÃ n Tranh
Description: A 16-string plucked zither used in Vietnamese classical and folk music. Related to the Chinese zheng family of instruments.

Name: Kannel / KanklÄ—s / Kokle
Description: A plucked psaltery-type zither found across the Baltic states. Each country's variant is considered a national instrument.

Name: Bandura
Description: A Ukrainian plucked string instrument with up to 68 strings. Associated with the kobzar tradition of blind itinerant epic singers.

Name: Ukulele
Description: A small four-stringed instrument developed in Hawaii from Portuguese immigrant instruments. Widely adopted across Pacific Island and global popular music.

Name: Banjo
Description: A stringed instrument with a drum-like body covered by a membrane. Developed by African Americans from West African lute traditions, central to bluegrass and folk music.

Name: Bouzouki
Description: A long-necked plucked lute with a round body and metal strings. The signature instrument of Greek rebetiko and popular music.

Name: Mandolin
Description: A small plucked string instrument with four paired courses of strings. Prominent in Italian, American bluegrass, and various European folk traditions.

Name: Harp (Celtic)
Description: A triangular frame harp with gut or nylon strings. A symbol of Irish and Scottish musical identity, with ancient roots in Celtic culture.

Name: Arpa Paraguaya
Description: A diatonic folk harp with a bright, cascading tone. The national instrument of Paraguay and central to guarania and polka paraguaya.

Name: Arpa Llanera
Description: A diatonic folk harp with a bright sound used in Venezuelan and Colombian joropo music. Played with rapid arpeggiated techniques.

Name: Mejorana
Description: A small five-stringed guitar from Panama used in tÃ­pico folk music. Carved from a single piece of wood.

Name: Mvet
Description: A stick zither and harp-zither from Central Africa (Cameroon, Gabon, Equatorial Guinea). Used to accompany epic oral narratives of the Fang people.

Name: Inanga
Description: A trough zither from Burundi and Rwanda. Used to accompany whispered narrative singing about historical events and legends.

Name: Qanun
Description: A large trapezoidal plucked zither with over 75 strings. A principal instrument in Arabic, Turkish, and Greek classical ensembles.

Name: Santur
Description: A hammered dulcimer with 72 strings struck with delicate wooden mallets. Central to Persian classical music and found across the Middle East and South Asia.

Name: Cimbalom
Description: A large concert hammered dulcimer played with padded beaters. Prominent in Hungarian, Romanian, and Central European folk and classical music.

Name: GuitarrÃ³n Mexicano
Description: A large, deep-bodied acoustic bass guitar. Provides the bass foundation in Mexican mariachi ensembles.

Name: Erhu
Description: A two-stringed bowed spike fiddle with a small resonator covered in python skin. One of the most popular Chinese traditional instruments.

Name: Morin Khuur
Description: A two-stringed Mongolian bowed fiddle with a carved horse-head scroll. The national instrument of Mongolia, traditionally associated with nomadic pastoral life.

Name: Kamancheh
Description: A bowed spike fiddle with a round body. A primary instrument in Persian, Azerbaijani, and broader Middle Eastern classical music.

Name: Sarangi
Description: A short-necked bowed instrument with gut strings and up to 40 sympathetic strings. Used in North Indian classical and Nepali folk music.

Name: Masinko
Description: A single-stringed bowed fiddle and one of the most common instruments in Ethiopian traditional music. Played by wandering minstrels called azmari.

Name: Gusle
Description: A single-stringed bowed instrument used to accompany epic poetry recitation in Serbia, Montenegro, Bosnia, and Croatia.

Name: Rebab
Description: A bowed string instrument found in varied forms across the Arab world, Southeast Asia, and Central Asia. Used in gamelan, Arab classical, and folk traditions.

Name: Hardanger Fiddle
Description: A Norwegian fiddle with four or five sympathetic resonating strings beneath the fingerboard. Produces a distinctive ringing, resonant tone used in folk music.

Name: Nyckelharpa
Description: A Swedish bowed instrument with keys (tangents) that change the pitch of the strings. Dates to medieval times and has been revived in the folk music scene.

Name: Gadulka
Description: A Bulgarian bowed string instrument with three melody strings and up to 10 sympathetic strings. Prominent in Bulgarian folk dance music.

Name: Saung Gauk
Description: A Burmese arched harp with 13 silk strings. One of the few surviving examples of the ancient arched harp tradition in Asia.

Name: ÄÃ n Báº§u
Description: A Vietnamese single-stringed monochord with a flexible pitch-bending rod. Produces ethereal, voice-like tones through harmonic techniques.

Name: Haegeum
Description: A Korean two-stringed vertical bowed fiddle. Used in both court and folk music ensembles.

Name: Berimbau
Description: A single-string percussion bow from Brazil, played by striking the string with a stick while using a gourd resonator. Inseparable from capoeira.

Name: Musical Bow
Description: A simple bowed or struck instrument found across Southern Africa, used by San, Zulu, and other peoples. One of the oldest string instruments in the world.

Name: Shakuhachi
Description: A Japanese end-blown bamboo flute with a distinctive breathy tone. Originally played by Zen Buddhist monks for meditation (suizen).

Name: Bansuri
Description: A transverse bamboo flute used in North Indian classical music. Produces a warm, rich tone central to Hindustani raga performance.

Name: Nay / Ney
Description: An end-blown reed flute used across the Middle East, Turkey, and Central Asia. One of the oldest musical instruments still in active use.

Name: Quena
Description: A notched end-blown flute made from cane or wood. The primary melodic instrument of Andean music across Peru, Bolivia, and Ecuador.

Name: Kaval
Description: An end-blown chromatic flute traditionally made from wood. Prominent in Bulgarian, Turkish, and broader Balkan shepherd music.

Name: Tin Whistle
Description: A simple six-hole fipple flute, also called a penny whistle. A signature instrument of Irish traditional music and widely used in Celtic traditions.

Name: Fujara
Description: A large Slovak overtone flute up to 1.8 meters long, played by shepherds in central Slovakia. Inscribed on UNESCO's intangible cultural heritage list.

Name: Washint
Description: An Ethiopian end-blown bamboo flute with four finger holes. Used in both solo performance and ensemble music.

Name: Suling
Description: A bamboo ring flute used across Indonesia and Malaysia. A key melodic instrument in Javanese and Balinese gamelan ensembles.

Name: Dizi
Description: A Chinese transverse bamboo flute with a distinctive buzzing membrane over one hole. Used in Chinese opera, folk, and orchestral music.

Name: Xiao
Description: A Chinese vertical end-blown bamboo flute with a gentle, mellow tone. Often paired with the guqin for intimate chamber music.

Name: Daegeum
Description: A large Korean transverse bamboo flute with a vibrating membrane, producing a rich buzzing quality. Used in court and folk music.

Name: Siku / ZampoÃ±a
Description: Panpipes made from rows of cane tubes of graduated length. Central to Andean music, traditionally played in interlocking pairs (ira and arka).

Name: Nai
Description: A Romanian curved panpipe made from bamboo or cane tubes. A virtuosic solo instrument in Romanian folk and classical music.

Name: Fangufangu
Description: A Tongan nose flute, played by directing breath from one nostril. Used in traditional Polynesian courtship music.

Name: KÅauau
Description: A small MÄori cross-blown flute traditionally made from bone, wood, or stone. Used for entertainment, mourning, and attracting birds.

Name: Rondador
Description: An Ecuadorian panpipe with tubes arranged in a zigzag pattern. Considered a national instrument of Ecuador.

Name: Salamuri
Description: A Georgian end-blown wooden flute with a warm tone. Used in both solo and ensemble folk music.

Name: Venu
Description: A South Indian bamboo transverse flute used in Carnatic classical music. Produces a sweet, clear tone across three octaves.

Name: Duduk
Description: A double-reed woodwind made from apricot wood, producing a warm, haunting sound. Armenia's national instrument, inscribed on UNESCO's list.

Name: Uilleann Pipes
Description: Irish bellows-blown bagpipes with a chanter, drones, and regulators. Capable of a wide range of dynamics and ornamentation, played seated.

Name: Gaita (Galician Bagpipe)
Description: A mouth-blown bagpipe from Galicia in northwestern Spain and northern Portugal. Central to Galician folk music and cultural identity.

Name: Gaida
Description: A Balkan bagpipe found across Bulgaria, North Macedonia, and Greece. Produces a piercing drone-and-melody sound used in folk dance music.

Name: Zurna / Sorna
Description: A loud double-reed oboe-type instrument played outdoors across Turkey, the Balkans, Central Asia, and the Middle East. Often paired with drums.

Name: Alghaita
Description: A West African double-reed wind instrument related to the zurna. Used in Hausa ceremonial music and across the Sahel.

Name: Mizmar
Description: A double-reed conical pipe from Egypt and the Levant. Used in folk celebrations, often paired with the tabla baladi.

Name: Shehnai
Description: A North Indian double-reed oboe with a flared bell. Traditionally played at weddings, temples, and auspicious ceremonies.

Name: Pi (Thai Oboe)
Description: A quadruple-reed oboe used in Thai classical piphat ensembles. Produces a nasal, penetrating tone that leads the melodic line.

Name: ChirimÃ­a
Description: A double-reed instrument of Spanish origin, adapted in Latin American indigenous and mestizo traditions. Still used in Guatemalan and Mexican ceremonial music.

Name: Gyaling
Description: A Tibetan double-reed oboe used in Buddhist monastery ceremonies. Produces a piercing, penetrating sound accompanying religious rituals.

Name: Khene
Description: A Lao mouth organ made from bamboo tubes fitted into a wooden windchest. The national instrument of Laos, central to lam and mor lam traditions.

Name: Sheng
Description: A Chinese free-reed mouth organ with vertical bamboo pipes arranged in a circle. One of the oldest polyphonic instruments in the world.

Name: ShÅ
Description: A Japanese free-reed mouth organ derived from the Chinese sheng. Used in gagaku court music to provide sustained harmonic clusters.

Name: Melodica
Description: A free-reed keyboard instrument blown through a mouthpiece. Popularized in Jamaican reggae and dub music, now used across genres worldwide.

Name: Harmonica
Description: A free-reed instrument played by blowing and drawing air across metal reeds. Central to blues, folk, country, and various global popular music traditions.

Name: Accordion
Description: A bellows-driven free-reed instrument with a keyboard or buttons. Foundational in tango, vallenato, zydeco, norteÃ±o, forrÃ³, musette, and many folk traditions worldwide.

Name: BandoneÃ³n
Description: A concertina-type bellows instrument with button keys on both sides. The signature sound of Argentine tango.

Name: Concertina
Description: A small bellows-driven free-reed instrument with buttons. Associated with Irish traditional, English folk, and South African music.

Name: Alphorn
Description: A long wooden horn originally used for communication across Alpine valleys. A symbol of Swiss pastoral culture, producing deep resonant tones.

Name: Didgeridoo (Yidaki)
Description: An Aboriginal Australian wind instrument made from a termite-hollowed eucalyptus trunk. One of the oldest wind instruments in the world, producing a continuous drone.

Name: Dungchen
Description: A Tibetan Buddhist long trumpet, sometimes over three meters in length. Used in monastery ceremonies, producing deep, resonant tones.

Name: Trembita
Description: A Ukrainian Carpathian alphorn made from a long, straight piece of spruce wood. Used by Hutsul shepherds for communication and ritual.

Name: Vuvuzela
Description: A long plastic horn that produces a loud monotone note. Became globally associated with South African football culture.

Name: PÅ«tÄtara
Description: A MÄori trumpet made from a conch shell fitted with a carved wooden mouthpiece. Used for signalling and ceremonial purposes in New Zealand.

Name: Vaksin
Description: Bamboo trumpets of various sizes used in Haitian rara processional music. Each player sounds a single note, creating interlocking melodic patterns.

Name: Djembe
Description: A goblet-shaped hand drum carved from a single piece of wood with a goat-skin head. Originating from the MandÃ© peoples of West Africa, now played globally.

Name: Tabla
Description: A pair of hand drums (treble dayan and bass bayan) used in North Indian classical music. Capable of extraordinary tonal variety and rhythmic complexity.

Name: Mridangam
Description: A double-headed barrel drum and the primary rhythmic instrument of South Indian (Carnatic) classical music. Produces a range of distinct tonal strokes.

Name: CajÃ³n
Description: A box-shaped drum of Afro-Peruvian origin, played by slapping the front face while seated on it. Now widely adopted in flamenco and global acoustic music.

Name: BodhrÃ¡n
Description: An Irish frame drum played with a double-ended beater (tipper). Central to Irish traditional music ensembles.

Name: Doira / Daf
Description: A large frame drum with metal rings inside the frame. Used across Central Asia, Iran, and the Middle East in both classical and folk music.

Name: Taiko
Description: A family of Japanese drums ranging from small hand drums to massive barrel drums. Played with wooden sticks (bachi) in ensemble performances of great physical energy.

Name: Janggu
Description: An hourglass-shaped Korean double-headed drum. A leading rhythmic instrument in Korean court music, folk music, and samulnori ensembles.

Name: Kendang
Description: A double-headed drum used across Indonesia and Malaysia. In gamelan, the kendang player directs the tempo and dynamics of the ensemble.

Name: Tabla Baladi
Description: An Egyptian goblet-shaped drum made of clay or metal, played with both hands. The primary hand drum of Egyptian folk and popular music.

Name: Tombak / Zarb
Description: An Iranian goblet drum carved from a single block of wood. Produces a wide range of tones and is central to Persian classical music rhythm.

Name: BatÃ¡
Description: A set of three hourglass-shaped double-headed drums sacred to the Yoruba LucumÃ­ tradition. Central to SanterÃ­a religious music in Cuba and Nigeria.

Name: Conga
Description: A tall, narrow single-headed Cuban drum of African origin, played with hands. A foundational instrument in salsa, Latin jazz, and Afro-Cuban music.

Name: Bongos
Description: A pair of small open-bottomed Cuban drums played between the knees. Prominent in son cubano, salsa, and Latin jazz.

Name: Timbales
Description: Shallow single-headed metal-shelled drums mounted on a stand, played with sticks. Central to salsa, mambo, and Latin dance music.

Name: Pandeiro
Description: A Brazilian frame drum with metal jingles, smaller than a tambourine. Essential to samba, choro, and many other Brazilian genres.

Name: Surdo
Description: A large bass drum carried by a strap during Brazilian Carnival. Provides the deep pulse in samba batucada drumming.

Name: Repinique
Description: A two-headed Brazilian tenor drum that leads and signals in samba batucada ensembles. Played with one stick and one hand.

Name: Talking Drum (Dundun)
Description: An hourglass-shaped drum whose pitch can be modulated by squeezing the lacing while striking. Used across West Africa for communication and music.

Name: Sabar
Description: A set of Wolof drums from Senegal, played with one hand and one stick. Central to mbalax and Wolof ceremonial music.

Name: Ingoma
Description: A large Burundian drum played in the Royal Drummers ensemble tradition. Made from a hollowed tree trunk with a stretched cowhide head.

Name: Tama
Description: A small Senegalese talking drum held under the arm and played with a curved stick. Capable of imitating the tonal patterns of the Wolof language.

Name: Madal
Description: A Nepali hand drum played horizontally across the lap. The most common folk drum in Nepal, used across many ethnic traditions.

Name: Kebero
Description: A double-headed Ethiopian drum used in both secular and Ethiopian Orthodox Church music. Played with bare hands.

Name: Ravanne
Description: A large Mauritian frame drum central to sÃ©ga music. Played over a fire to tighten the goat-skin head, then struck with hands.

Name: RoulÃ©r
Description: A barrel drum from RÃ©union, central to maloya music. Placed between the legs and played with both hands.

Name: Tambora
Description: A double-headed drum played with a stick on one side and bare hand on the other. The rhythmic foundation of Dominican merengue.

Name: Steelpan
Description: A melodic percussion instrument made from oil drums, invented in Trinidad in the mid-20th century. The only major acoustic instrument created in the 20th century.

Name: Kundu
Description: An hourglass-shaped drum from Papua New Guinea, carved from wood and covered with lizard skin. Central to sing-sing ceremonial performances.

Name: Pate
Description: A slit drum carved from a log, found across Polynesia. Used for signaling and rhythmic accompaniment in Samoan and Tongan music.

Name: Boduberu
Description: A coconut-wood drum covered with goat or ray skin from the Maldives. Played in ensembles for the boduberu call-and-response tradition.

Name: Doira
Description: A Central Asian frame drum prominent in Uzbek and Tajik music. Played with rapid finger techniques producing complex rhythmic patterns.

Name: Gamelan Ensemble
Description: A large ensemble of predominantly bronze metallophones, gongs, and drums from Java and Bali, Indonesia. One of the world's most sophisticated orchestral traditions.

Name: Balafon
Description: A West African wooden xylophone with gourd resonators. Central to MandÃ© musical traditions and inscribed on UNESCO's list.

Name: Mbira (Kalimba)
Description: An African lamellophone (thumb piano) with metal tines mounted on a wooden board. Central to Shona spiritual music and found across the continent in many forms.

Name: Marimba
Description: A large wooden-barred percussion instrument with tubular resonators. Important in Central American, Mexican, and Southern African musical traditions.

Name: Kulintang
Description: A row of horizontally laid small gongs in a frame, played with wooden beaters. Central to the musical traditions of the southern Philippines and Borneo.

Name: Angklung
Description: An Indonesian instrument made of bamboo tubes attached to a frame, shaken to produce notes. Traditionally played in large communal ensembles; inscribed on UNESCO's list.

Name: Ranat Ek
Description: A Thai wooden xylophone and the lead melodic instrument in classical piphat ensembles. Played with two padded mallets at rapid speed.

Name: Khong Wong Yai
Description: A Thai gong circle consisting of 16 bossed gongs in a rattan frame. Provides the fundamental melody in piphat ensembles.

Name: Amadinda
Description: A Ugandan log xylophone played by three interlocking performers simultaneously. Studied for its complex polyphonic technique.

Name: Timbila
Description: A Mozambican xylophone of the Chopi people, played in large orchestral ensembles. Inscribed on UNESCO's list for its compositional sophistication.

Name: Slit Drum (Garamut)
Description: A hollowed log struck to produce tones, used across Melanesia, Africa, and the Americas. Historically used for long-distance communication.

Name: Cajita
Description: A small wooden box struck with a mallet, used in Afro-Peruvian music. One of several improvised percussion instruments in the tradition.

Name: GÃ¼ira
Description: A cylindrical metal scraper from the Dominican Republic. Provides a driving rhythmic texture in merengue alongside the tambora.

Name: Maracas
Description: Gourd or shell rattles filled with seeds or beads. Used across Latin America and the Caribbean, prominent in salsa, cumbia, and joropo.

Name: Kayamb
Description: A flat rattle from RÃ©union made from sugarcane flower stalks filled with seeds. A defining instrument of maloya and sÃ©ga music.

Name: Caxixi
Description: A small woven basket rattle from Brazil, typically played alongside the berimbau in capoeira. Adds rhythmic texture to the berimbau's sound.

Name: AgogÃ´
Description: A set of two or more coned metal bells struck with a stick, originating from Yoruba tradition. Used in Brazilian samba and West African ceremonial music.

Name: Claves
Description: A pair of short cylindrical hardwood sticks struck together. Provide the rhythmic timeline (clave pattern) in Cuban and Latin American music.

Name: Castanets
Description: A pair of concave wooden shells clicked together by the fingers. Associated with Spanish flamenco and broader Iberian folk traditions.

Name: Piano
Description: A large keyboard instrument where hammers strike steel strings. One of the most versatile and widely played instruments in Western classical, jazz, pop, and many global traditions.

Name: Organ (Pipe)
Description: A keyboard instrument producing sound by sending pressurized air through pipes. Central to Western sacred music for centuries, from cathedrals to gospel churches.

Name: Harmonium
Description: A small bellows-driven keyboard instrument pumped by hand or foot. Widely adopted in South Asian music, particularly in devotional, qawwali, and Hindustani classical settings.

Name: Celesta
Description: A keyboard instrument that strikes metal plates with hammers, producing a delicate bell-like tone. Used in orchestral and film music for ethereal effects.

Name: Synthesizer
Description: An electronic instrument that generates audio signals to create a wide range of sounds. Foundational to electronic, pop, hip-hop, and experimental music since the 1960s.

Name: Drum Machine
Description: An electronic device that produces drum and percussion sounds via synthesis or samples. Fundamental to hip-hop, electronic dance music, and modern pop production.

Name: Turntable
Description: A phonograph record player used as a musical instrument through scratching and beat juggling. Pioneered in hip-hop DJ culture and now used across electronic genres.

Name: Theremin
Description: An electronic instrument played without physical contact, using hand proximity to two antennas to control pitch and volume. Invented in Russia in 1920.

Name: Electric Guitar
Description: A solid or semi-hollow body guitar with magnetic pickups and electronic amplification. Defined rock, blues, jazz, and countless popular music genres since the mid-20th century.

Name: Electric Bass Guitar
Description: A bass-range electric stringed instrument. Provides the low-end foundation in rock, funk, jazz, pop, and most modern popular music.

Name: Sampler
Description: A device or software that records and plays back audio samples, allowing them to be manipulated and sequenced. Central to hip-hop, electronic, and contemporary production.

Name: Khoomei (Throat Singing)
Description: A Mongolian and Tuvan vocal technique where a single singer simultaneously produces two or more pitches. Inscribed on UNESCO's list.

Name: Yodeling
Description: A singing technique involving rapid alternation between chest and head voice. Found in Alpine European, Central African Pygmy, and various other traditions independently.

Name: Beatboxing
Description: A vocal percussion technique that imitates drum machines, turntables, and other sounds using the mouth, lips, tongue, and voice. Originated in hip-hop culture.

Name: Katajjaq (Inuit Throat Singing)
Description: A vocal game from the Inuit peoples of Canada and Greenland, performed by two women facing each other, producing rhythmic guttural sounds in alternation.

Name: Canto a Tenore
Description: A Sardinian form of polyphonic singing with four voice parts, one imitating natural and animal sounds. Inscribed on UNESCO's list.

Name: Joik
Description: The traditional vocal expression of the SÃ¡mi people of northern Scandinavia. A personal, evocative form of singing that portrays people, animals, or landscapes.

Name: Kulning
Description: A Scandinavian herding call using a high-pitched vocal technique to carry across mountain valleys. Historically used by women to call livestock.
